utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good morning to you. I notice that the accused Pandurevic is not present. I'm informed he had a dental appointment or appointment with a dentist and that he should be brought back here at about 9.40. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He's here represented by counsel. He's going to miss a few minutes of evidence. We can talk to him about that in the break. We are content the matter should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes. If there are problems with interpretation, let me know. Otherwise I see again Mr. Bourgon is not here. Anything wrong with Mr. Bourgon or is he --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have the interpretation. But basically he is okay. He is working. And he should be back. I see that there is Mr. Nicholls and Mr. McCloskey. Okay. Let's -- any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly Your Honours. I wanted to address you before the witness comes in. Good morning, first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if they are before you now but we've passed out two booklets to each of you. Those have been shown to my friends on the other side and there has been no objection. The first one is a book of still images extracted from some of the video I plan to show today. Those are from an exhibit, number 65 ter 1936, and the purpose of that is to assist in following the video, who is who, who we'll see on the video. I don't intend to show that to the witness. It's just that it may, I thought, aid the Trial Chamber in following the videos. And the second is a map book which, again, there has been no objection. I do not plan to use the map book today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's make this clear. This you are not going to use with the witness, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of these stills here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. There is a possibility I will use some stills with the witness but they are not labelled in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was aiming at to make sure that if you make use of this, that there are no indications corresponding to the numbers that are shown against figures. All right. Any comments from the Defence? I see here none, so let's bring in Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. Today we will be proceeding with your examination-in-chief. So I leave you in the very capable hands of Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. First of all, I want to ask you just a couple of follow-up questions from the last time we spoke here. On page 1898, line 1 of the transcript last time, we were talking about how when you went on patrol, shells which you -- which from the VRS were landing about 50 metres away from your Mercedes. And you said: "I assumed that this originated from VRS. Initially there had been a report about -- from the UN interpreter Petar in Bratunac who indicated that it was dangerous to regularly come in-bound as we were doing with vehicles. So this was a warning to beware." Could you please explain just a little bit more about how you took this to be a warning and about what Petar told you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpreted this as a clear warning, and I personally decided that only in dire emergencies would I leave the camp, and I would not go on patrols without good reason. I assumed that this message was sincere and was a warning to beware.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told us that Petar was an interpreter. Do you recall his last name?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that, but I would certainly recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is Petar?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him explicitly, but he resided in Bratunac and had extensive freedom of movement there and he seemed to be on good terms with the local population, so I assume he was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which organisation actually employed him as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked for the UN. Interpreters were deployed both in and outside the enclave, that is to say UN interpreters, and this interpreter was assigned to the Serbian side and was paid by the UN. So I assume he was on the UN payroll.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I understand you correctly, he could travel freely between the enclave and Bratunac where he lived?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not residing in the enclave. He resided somewhere in Bratunac. So he certainly wasn't circulating about the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question wasn't clear but I think you've answered it well. Also last time you indicated at page 1899 of the transcript that you did tell Momir Nikolic about the VRS shelling near your vehicle that you've described again this morning. I forgot to ask you what his response was when you -- when you told him about that shelling. Could you tell us now?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically remember his reaction. The only thing that sticks vaguely in the back of my mind is that he indicated that this is part of the game, you have to watch out and take care and don't get into dangerous situations unnecessarily. And another time I was heading toward Yellow Bridge for a discussion. I was told, "You have a few minutes to leave, and if you don't head back toward the enclave we are going to have to shoot you because you have no reason to be here anymore. This is part of your instructions." And you could see that -- you could place his reaction in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was it who said that to you? That if you didn't leave you would be shot at.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the guards at Yellow Bridge, one of the VRS soldiers, sometime in June. He was quite sincere. I knew the individual relatively well, and he was somewhat uncomfortable too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move back to where we left off and you had begun to describe events on the 10th of July when you said the population began moving towards Potocari. Can you describe that journey of the population and what you observed as the population moved from Srebrenica to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was staying in the compound or the headquarters of the Bravo company in Srebrenica. Occasionally, that is to say two or three times, I walked -- I took a short walk through the city. It was about a few hundred metres to the UN post. Also -- there was also a postal station and I would get an impression of what was happening. There was a general sentiment of panic. People didn't know what to do. It was unsafe. The military leadership had the same feeling. Ramiz Becirevic contacted us and asked us to guarantee his safety. Overall, I wasn't in direct contact, but I was indirectly in contact with the MSF staff and the hospital, and they said that the situation was becoming too dangerous for them, and they asked whether we might be able to transport the injured in the hospital toward Potocari. So there was a general feeling that it was unsafe. They didn't feel that the people in Srebrenica could protect them very well, and they were -- they wondered whether they could go to the headquarters for -- in search of safety, and they said perhaps we should head toward Potocari. I think that that feeling spread, and it was instigated by the population or the leadership. Whether it was the military, civilian authorities or by DutchBat, I don't remember exactly who instigated it, but the people were basically feeling as if they were hunted. That was my first impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you make that journey to -- from Bravo company to Charlie company in Potocari yourself?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At a certain point, when a considerable share of the Bravo company was already travelling in vehicles, I got into a Mercedes and drove in that direction down a narrow road filled with people, heading toward Potocari, on foot, some were staggering along, some were carrying a few bags. They were proceeding slowly along the road and to the left and the right, and there were shots but not very -- not a very close range. So they felt that the situation was unsafe. They would look around very nervously and they would hear the shots and the general feeling was we should go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And by shots, do you mean shelling or what kind of shots does that refer to? It says "shots" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean a combination of firearms, rifles, machine-guns, and occasional shelling, of mortars, that was audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could just remind us of the distance between Srebrenica and Potocari, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose about three or four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'd like you, if you can, to describe the scene at Potocari when you arrived, what you saw there, how many people you think gathered around the compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a huge mass of people. They were waiting there aimlessly. On the road from Potocari towards Srebrenica, there is some old garages with gates in front of them, and they opened the gates and people tried to find a place to sit in the shade, if possible, because it was quite hot. Here and there you would see a small well and people carrying water. If you ask me how many people there were, a lot. I can't estimate the number but certainly thousands, several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if I could hear either from you or from Colonel what an MSF is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, he stated that on his first day of testimony, Your Honours, that's Medecins Sans Frontieres, Doctors Without Borders, I believe. But the witness could confirm that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's Medecins Sans Frontieres, meaning Doctors Without Borders. And that was an organisation supporting the hospital in the enclave and also running little health clinics inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us briefly now what there was available to provide for all these people in Potocari, whether there was food available, how much, whether there was water available, how much, for these thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the people themselves had very limited amount of baggage that they were carrying. Occasionally they would have a jug of water, a tiny little bit of food, emergency rations that they could carry in their hands. So they were able to provide limited supplies for themselves. As far as what DutchBat could do for so many people, very little. Our supplies were limited too. At a certain point, we assessed how much we had. We figured out that this would last only a few days until we could no longer provide for ourselves and the people, perhaps two or three days. If we were to tap into our own supplies, they would be exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You mentioned that DutchBat agreed to take some patients from MSF to Potocari. Do you recall how many patients were brought to Potocari and what -- whether -- what type of care was provided for them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of -- the number of patients is something I haven't witnessed myself. I assumed this to be in the tens, maybe a little bit less than 100. As to the care provided, there was a medical team, some surgeons. They were present at the first aid post. And therefore, they would able to provide first aid assistance, but they were very limited in the additional care they could provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you talked about hearing shots of a variety of weapons in Srebrenica. Once you were in Potocari, could you still hear shots of shelling or other types of arms?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This could be heard. There was continuous fire with short interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just so you could tell us, were you aware of any shells coming anywhere near, near the UN compound in Potocari at this time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall this with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We've now described the situation leading up to 11th of July. I'd like to talk now about what you did and where you went on the 11th of July. And first of all, did you attend a meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If here you mention a first meeting that took place in Bratunac, then this was a meeting where Commander Karremans and the Sergeant-Major Rave and myself attended, and yes, I did attend this meeting. A number of Serbians were present, both military personnel and civilian representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was this meeting held in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took place at the hotel bar I knew well, Fontana, the Fontana Hotel in the city of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did this meeting come about? Who requested or arranged the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the past, questions have been asked about this several times, here in The Hague. I cannot recall exactly what my answer was then. However, at the present time, I cannot precisely indicate whether the initiative had come from the VRS or the DutchBat side. In any case, it was a meeting where we arrived, where we were welcomed, and where we were expected. People were expecting us in order to hold the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: And during the first meeting, we had to pass by VRS soldiers that were marching towards the enclave and therefore the situation was not completely safe. However, at the moments that we would be stopped by these soldiers, we would be granted permission to travel on. There was communication through walkie-talkies, and therefore I assumed that the meeting had been set up and that they knew about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What time of day was the meeting? Let me put it this way: When did you arrive at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the course of the afternoon, maybe the early evening. I cannot recall the precise time. I would have to look into my previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think early evening -- I'm most interested in what you can remember now. Now, besides yourself, Commander Karremans and Sergeant-Major Rave, did anybody else come from the DutchBat side?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the delegation that travelled by car towards the meeting, no. What I can recall is that at the Hotel Fontana, when one enters, I noticed a number of Dutchmen in a room as you enter, to the right. They were waiting. I then entered into the room and discovered that these were some of the DutchBat troops that had been taken prisoner and that were present there under guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about those DutchBat prisoners a little bit later. As best as you remember, who was present at the meeting from the VRS side, the military?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the military side of the VRS were present General Mladic, Colonel Jankovic, Major Momir Nikolic, and I also believe that General Krstic was present. Petar the interpreter was present as well. I believe that, as far as I could see, those were the main participants in the meeting at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'd like to now show you some video footage we have of that meeting, that may, I imagine, help you remember the meeting and then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe the number is 1992 for the first Hotel Fontana meeting, and I'm actually going to try to stop it quite soon after it starts for the witness to take a look at what we see. May I sit down so that I can see the screen better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Can you see the screen in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just going from left to right in the picture we see which is 00:37:00:5, can you tell us who we see, these five men, left to right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, Colonel Jankovic, Commander Karremans, Sergeant-Major Rave, and we see a little bit of myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe since it's been so short we could start it again and now just watch the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Two things. First of all, with reference to page 11, line 16, the witness identified General Mladic, Colonel Jankovic, Commander Karremans, Sergeant-Major Rave and a little bit of himself at still 36:36:4. And while the video was being shown, the accused Pandurevic was admitted in the courtroom, roughly at 8 minutes to 10.00. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could look at the screen, a man just entered the screen. We are at 00:40:05.5. He's got his back to us. He's wearing a striped shirt. Can you identify who that man is?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is Petar, the UN interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, where it stopped it's slightly blurry but we are at 01:14:43.7, General Mladic said, "Zile, come here," and then this man comes in and has a toast with General Mladic. Do you know who the man is who has come in the screen? He's in the forefront on the right of the screen having a toast with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clearly visible. That could be General Zivanovic but I can't see clearly at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll keep playing it and maybe later you'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before we keep on playing, how much longer --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's very nearly done, Your Honour, perhaps a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's finish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is the end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First question, Colonel: How did you feel during this meeting that we've just watched?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't feel like an equal. It was like I was threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- well, what did you feel threatened with? Could you explain to us a bit more what you mean you feel threatened, you felt threatened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, during the meeting, it wasn't possible to follow everything because first of all the interpreter was standing closer to Colonel Karremans than to me, and if you consider the situation, some of our own soldiers had been taken prisoner and I met those and spoke with them briefly. And then after that, I entered the meeting where Colonel Karremans was talking to General Mladic, and I noticed that people were being pushed into a corner and General Mladic was using threatening language and was trying to impress them and threatening that if air support were used again, then saying, "We can do as we please with you." And the joke, "This needn't be your last cigarette" clearly sets the tone that, "I'm in charge here." And that disregarding the situation of the refugees that I had just left, who were -- we were unable to meet their primary needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just describe now what you said in your last answer, you noticed that people were being pushed into a corner? Who was pushing whom and did you become involved in any physical pushing yourself?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- from the VRS, the body-guard and some other soldiers nearby were trying to drive Colonel Karremans into a corner, both literally and metaphorically. And when I arrived a bit later I noticed that and I tried to make some space.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that's not shown on the videotape of the meeting we've seen, is it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct. Not everything was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From what you -- from what we've seen, does the recording appear to be a fair and accurate recording of the meeting, although not of all of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it does a reasonable job conveying the duration of the meeting and the tenor of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We stopped on a slightly blurry frame before the break, and you said that you thought, I don't have your exact words, but that the person in the picture could have been General Zivanovic. Having seen a little bit more of the video, are you able to say whether or not that person was General Zivanovic, the one who comes in and has a toast with General Mladic and then with the rest of the persons present?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture was too blurred for me. Whether it's Zivanovic or Krstic, I would be guessing. So I'm not going to make any statements about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You recalled in the beginning that Momir Nikolic was present at this meeting but you didn't identify him on the video. Was he off camera or was he -- do you -- best as you can, was he present at the meeting, just not seen on the video?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he would probably have been at the beginning of the meeting, to receive us at the entrance, and perhaps he was present when we entered. But other than that, he did not figure significantly in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to see the film crew from where you were standing in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A film crew was walking around with a camera, and they held the camera very close to the faces of the people being recorded. The camera was very clearly present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you recall, how were they dressed? In civilian or military clothing? The film crew.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a very vague memory, but I suspect that it was a combination. They certainly were wearing some civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in the Krstic trial, over six years ago, you mentioned another person from the VRS present at the meeting. Would it help you remember who else might be there if I were to show you that portion of your transcript?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't imagine it would do any harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from page 1165 of the Krstic transcript. You were shown a photograph which was Exhibit 28/5.1 in that trial, in the Prosecution, and you said -- you were asked if you recognised the person in the photograph and you said: "Yes, I do recognise that man. He was also during the meeting there. He was busy with the transport and organisation to bring out the Muslim people to Kladanj later on." And this portion of the transcript concerned the first meeting. You were then asked: "Do you know what he's called?" And you answered: "Kosovic or something like that." Just think about that for a minute, and I want to see if that helps you to remember whether there was a VRS officer there with a name that you said is "Kosovic or something like that"?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosoric, Kosovic is what I remember. A person -- I would recognise him if I saw a picture of him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. In --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm asking you from your memory now, do you remember this officer being present at the first meeting, although he was not on the video we just saw?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were others present and especially if I review the statement from a few years ago, I stand behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now just jump out of order a bit and show a short clip. This is from the third -- well, I won't say what it's from. It says it on the screen. The third meeting at the Hotel Fontana and we'll stop it quite soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the video starts playing at 01:42:51.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could play a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about using this picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We will get to that, Your Honour. There is a shot I was thinking of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me, if you recognise the man on the far right in this picture facing towards us?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see him. And that's the man we were talking about, Mr. Kosovic or Kosoric or something like that, who was responsible for transporting the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that. I'm sorry. That's at 01:42:51.9. I'd like to know show you another brief video and see if you recognise where it is and the people on the video. This is 65 ter number 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we need to put this in the record. So the video that has been played starts at 1:01:41.37, and stops at 01:42:42.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the men on that video?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some from DutchBat who, so to speak, were being held prisoner by the VRS at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you recognise where they were being held from that, from that video, the room? Did you recognise the room or where that video was shot?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No. [Interpretation] It could have been recorded at the Fontana in Bratunac but the rooms resemble each other a lot. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you described it but just to be clear, did you personally see and talk to the hostages at the Hotel Fontana when you were there on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, at the start of the first meeting, when I entered one -- there was a room like that to my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already stated that, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wanted to be sure, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what did you do after the first meeting, the long meeting video we have watched?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove back to the camp at Potocari, and we tried to find a representative of the population or of the military, and ultimately we found a former teacher that I knew. We managed to find him among the group of people, and he agreed to act as a spokesman for the population. We involved him in preparing the next meeting, the same day, at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 11.00 at night or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the same day as the first meeting, which we've already watched the video of?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the first meeting, did you discuss at all with Commander Karremans how he felt after that meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine it was brief. He also wanted to report to his superiors about how the meeting went and to prepare for the next conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to start talking now about your return to Bratunac for the second meeting scheduled for 11.00 p.m. First of all, who from DutchBat travelled to the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac for the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Karremans, Nesib Mandic [phoen], not of DutchBat but for the population, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Nesib Mandic, just to be clear, is that the name of the school teacher you said that was selected to come back with you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you travel to Bratunac for the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my own Mercedes, and I believe that Mandic was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were there any stops or incidents along the way to the Hotel Fontana for the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we stopped at least once or twice on the way. They checked who was in the car, and there was some threatening sentiment about, "Who do you have with you? What are you doing here?" It was difficult for me to understand them because I didn't have an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, who is the "they" who checked out who was in the car?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serb soldiers, or in any case, troops that had joined the VRS in the offensive against the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the Hotel Fontana for the second meeting, as best you can recall, who was there from the VRS side present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mladic was certainly there; Nikolic at the start; and, well, I believe General Krstic was present as well; Colonel Jankovic; and at this time I don't remember who else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember -- do you remember if there were any civilians present at the meeting, other than Nesib Mandic who you brought with you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three civilians were also present. They worked for the police or the Bratunac authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just say for the transcript it's Nesib Mandzic, not Mandic. And just to be very clear, what was the ethnicity of Mr. Mandzic? Was he a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That already emerges clear from your previous question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, before we play the videotape, there is a strange loud noise we hear in the background at some point. Can you tell us what that is so I don't -- if you recall, so I don't have to stop it while we are at that point while we are playing it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a sound that an animal might have been slaughtered. It was a screeching.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think we could play the video now. This is 65 ter number 1994, and I will stop it at several points to see if the witness recognises people on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Before it gets going too far, can you just tell us who we see here, again from left to right, just sitting around the table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before he answers that question -- one moment, Colonel, one moment. Pardon me. The video starts at 01:16:09.5. And the question that has just been put to Colonel Boering refers to still at 01:16:18.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, if you could tell us who you recognise, not the man standing up at the moment but just sitting around the table, left to right as we look at the picture?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the left you see Colonel Jankovic. To his right is the interpreter, Petar. And then Lieutenant Colonel Karremans and you can see half of Nesib Mandzic. And in the background, is General Mladic's body-guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we play the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've asked Janet to stop the video at 01:19:05.2. Colonel, do you recognise the man in this picture?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed, the noise or the sound of what allegedly is an animal starts at 01:18:05, right through 01:18:18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is no sound in our ear phones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a problem that Mr. Lazarevic only is encountering or are the rest of you? You all have the same problem? You are okay? You're okay? You're not. So we need to adjust this. Could it just be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we all have the problem because the accused need to hear the text in B/C/S in order to be able to understand. So this is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, Ms. Nikolic. This is why I said stop and let's address this problem. Starting with the accused, have you been able to follow? Could you hear? But they didn't encounter the problem before when we had the previous video. We didn't hear the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, did you follow the English channel or B/C/S channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was able to follow this on B/C/S up until the moment when it stopped and then after that, the sound just stopped and we heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as far as the accused, I recognise General Miletic saying that he couldn't follow. General Gvero as well; Nikolic as well; Pandurevic; Beara, no; and Popovic. So we need to address this problem. I mean, the accused must be in a position where they can sit and follow the conversation. My apologies to you, Colonel Boering. We are trying to accelerate the momentum as much as we can so that you can go home but when you try to do that, you end up with problems. Is a technician on his way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can go back a few images or -- let's say, and first we give it a try to see whether you are receiving the sound. If not, we will proceed with interpretation, live interpretation, in other words. Would that be acceptable to the various Defence teams? So let's -- Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think to do that it would be much better to make transcripts available to the booths. We can do it for them, and I don't have that many now. I would prefer if we can try to fix it so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- hear the voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be my first preference, too, because also the intonation sometimes is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, I think to get the sense of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know exactly what you mean. I've occupied your place before. So Madam Registrar, if you could kindly summon the technicians to come and check? In the meantime, can we play back a part of it and see whether it's working now. If you could kindly also adjust because sometimes it's just the wire that is attached to the socket that needs a little bit of adjustment. Okay. We can start from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A little bit silly, but just for the record who do we see on the screen here at 01:21:21.3?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop it again for a while but this is a better shot than before. Who is the man we see on the screen at 01:21:36.6?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Sergeant-Major Rave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed. One moment. I just want to confirm for the record that now you can follow the video and that the sound is okay. Including the accused? Yes, I see everyone nodding. I thank you. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the video was stopped at 01:42:31.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have the same question for you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you put the question, let's clear this from my mind, Mr. Nicholls. The reason why I'm putting the question to Colonel Boering is because previously you asked him whether what he saw on the screen was a faithful representation of the actual meeting. That was the first one. Now we have the second. I checked while this was going on, whether there was any interpretation in Dutch. There was interpretation in French but there was no interpretation in Dutch. I wouldn't imagine that there were difficulties for the witness, for Colonel Boering, but I just want a confirmation from him that he could follow completely the entire video, both this one and the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the reason is that apparently he's chosen to -- not to follow the proceedings in English but in Dutch, and this was only in Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you understood the President's concerns and question, Colonel, were you able to follow the videos we have been watching in English? Is your English good enough to understand what we have been listening to and seeing on the subtitles?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've been able to follow it completely in English. My choice to prefer Dutch in the court proceedings was that this -- the fact to speak in my native language helps me to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls, and thank you Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, during this second meeting, how did you feel as you sat there in the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, once again, there was the language problem, especially the part where General Mladic spoke directly to Nesib Mandzic. I sat to the left of Nesib Mandzic and next to Mandzic was Karremans and next to him the interpreter, so I couldn't follow the part that was directly in the local language. I did understand the general gist. A desperate situation, in trying to -- trying to make clear that we wanted to leave the enclave and that there were no prospects for better support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And during the portion of the meeting where there was that loud, high-pitched kind of screaming sound that you said you thought was an animal being killed, how did -- did you wonder what that was? How did that make you feel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The videotape we've seen, I know that you couldn't hear all of the conversation between General Mladic and Mr. Mandzic during, as it happened, but does the video appear to you to be an accurate and fair recording of the meeting, as much of it as was captured on videotape?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of the meeting was taped. But as far as I remember, the highlights are visible in these shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How much more of the meeting do you recall was there that we haven't been able to see here today? And I can say if it helps that the video clip we've seen is approximately 20 minutes, if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps about ten minutes was not played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you remember, if you know, what did that ten minutes -- what was going on during those ten minutes, just generally?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That isn't rock solid in my memory at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you one more question that you may or may not remember. Was this person you identified as a VRS officer Kosovic or Kosoric, was he present at this meeting, the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to show a still from the meeting. This is 65 ter number 0452. This is General Mladic asked that a sign -- somebody off camera, he says, "Can you get that sign?" And then he says in the clip we've seen, "Put it down in front of Nesib." And he says, "He got it himself from the town hall." Do you recognise the still that's before you? And sorry, let me say for the record it's 01038810 is the ERN number. Do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember it being carried in and presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your mind, what was the effect of putting this broken part of the sign from the town hall of Srebrenica down on the table in front of the Muslim representative?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this is my personal interpretation, but it clearly conveyed that you're no longer in charge in your city. We are in charge now. And that message hit home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the meeting was over, did the DutchBat members who were there and Nesib Mandzic travel back to Potocari together?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove back with Nesib Mandzic in my car, and I believe that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans drove back with Sergeant-Major Rave. We went in two different cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, as -- after the meeting, what was Nesib Mandzic's demeanour? How was he feeling after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wondered whether going there had been the right thing. He was worried whether he had taken the right position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I am not receiving interpretation of what you're saying, Mr. Krgovic. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning because this is speculation. The witness is being asked to say how someone else felt, but he also mentioned in the previous answer that he did not have an interpreter when he was going back with Nesib Mandzic, so what he's saying now then about that is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether it's speculation or not I have my doubts, but I suppose you need to rephrase the series of questions starting with the basic one whether he could at the time going back to the compound have a conversation, an intelligible conversation with Mr. Mandzic, and then the next one would be of course whether he discussed with Mr. Mandzic his own feeling about, and then you can proceed from there. But the main point raised by Mr. Krgovic is a valid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to communicate with Nesib Mandzic on the way back from the meeting at all? And if you could, how could you do that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication was limited, in English, or German. I don't remember exactly anymore, but it was limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I was asking you about --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: But later, we were back at the compound in Potocari, and an interpreter was present there, and then I was able to speak with him briefly. So it was a combination of during the drive and upon arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I was asking and I probably didn't ask it well, was in the first question, based on just common sense, human experience, were you able to see people and see how they looked to us, whether they look happy, sad, tired, scared, how did he appear to you as another human being as you drove back?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frightened, insecure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's clear this up. Did he specifically ask him how he felt about the meeting? At least when he could have a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Once you were back at Potocari and you were able to speak with interpretation, did Mr. Mandzic tell you how he felt about -- how he had felt during the meeting and how he felt about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I spoke to him about that briefly, and he expressed his feelings, "What should I do? I don't know how to continue from here. I need more representatives to provide backup in the meeting at 10.00, so I need more support as a representative." So I remember that we spoke about it in those terms and then he went off to look for an expansion to the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now. It's number 0531, a fax from Commander Karremans. It should appear on your screen in a minute, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, Your Honour, I should know this again but I'm not sure how we get it, if the accused want to see it in their language, if it can be brought up for them in B/C/S. There is a translation we have provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to refer to specific parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I am, and I can read out these parts in English and it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can deal with it like that. You don't have a B/C/S? They cannot. Okay. All right. So if you're going to refer to any particular parts of this document, please explain what it is so that the accused can have an interpretation in their language with a view to knowing what document we are talking about, and if there are specific -- references to specific parts, please read the relevant part so that it can be translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was able to find translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They cannot. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought we could do a split screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is something that should be arranged. I mean, I can't understand why we, who don't need to see much the version in Serbo-Croat of documents unless we are looking at signatures, which is not the case here, can see it, and the accused, who have got a vested interest in all this cannot. Do you have a hard copy of the document in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I do, Your Honour. I'm sorry. We have it in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's make it a practice that in such cases at least you will have these documents readily available in hard copy because we can put them on the ELMO and the accused will be able to follow from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My suggestion, Your Honour, would be I think we are five minutes from the break. I'll bring in hard copies in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine, fine. Good idea. Perfect. I think a combination of minds, that's what you get. We'll have a break now. I take it you are going to finish today? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It will be close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you now that you have practically heard the almost -- the whole testimony of Colonel Boering, revise your cross-examination estimates and communicate it to the court registrar and to Mr. Nicholls so that more or less we can give an indication to Colonel Boering when he can go home and when we can have the next witness. All right? Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that the problem that we referred to before has been solved, and that it is now possible to see on the screen, on the monitor, on the left-hand side the English version of the document, and on the right-hand side its corresponding translation into B/C/S. So that should prove helpful to the accused who can now definitely follow better. I thank the staff for taking the initiative to get this done. I've said it mainly for the record so that it's on the record that we can see we both. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, are you able to read the document in English on the screen in front of you or would you like me to give you a hard copy to look at which I can show the Defence, if that is better for you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'd like a hard copy as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could show this to counsel first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, please take a minute or as long as you need, read that entire two-page document to yourself, Colonel, and then I'll ask you some questions. I'll say now for the record this has ERN numbers R0015489 through 5490. I'll also ask you Colonel, while you're reading that, if you recall that you saw this document when we first met last week?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. Yes. I've read both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me. If we can go back to the first page, please. Thank you. Sir, we can see that this is from the commanding officer, DutchBat, compound Potocari, Srebrenica, in the top right-hand corner. And we see a date in the top left-hand corner and time of 12 July 1995, 0335. And it is addressed to force Commander Janvier, commander BH command, HQ UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, commander Sector North-East, the Ministry of Defence here in The Hague and to -- something, I'm not completely sure what this is, the Crisis Staff Den Haag, Den Haag here. So, first of all, the second address it just says commander Bosnia-Herzegovina command, Sarajevo. Who would receive this at that command at this time, if you know? Who would be a commander?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Dutch representative there, General Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see that the subject is the meeting with General Mladic on the 11th and 12th July 1995. I don't want to ask you too much about the first page, which I think is fairly self-explanatory. If we could go to the second page now, point 5. "There are more than 15.000 people within one square kilometre, including the battalion, in an extreme vulnerable position, the sitting duck position, not able to defend these people at all. In direct line and above the compound, he deployed two guns, two tanks, three MLRs and one AA gun, all in direct sight. At this moment, I'm responsible for these people." Could you comment on this section, first, as based on your military experience whether you share the same assessment made by Karremans or a different one, that would be my first question, that this was a difficult position.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This description is accurate. With what we had, we could do little against this type of armament and deployment. As said, that turns you into a sitting duck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what an MLR is, or an MLRS, what type of weapon that is?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's a multi-launch rocket system. [Interpretation] It's an artillery type that fires multiple grenades that spread shards very effectively across an area. Suppose you fire an MLRS at civilians sitting in a field, you'll have a lot of casualties and injured, if you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, what is an AA gun, as it's referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume this means an anti-aircraft, so against airplanes and targets in the air. But you can also -- you can also shoot them at people or vehicles. You can aim them directly as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Moving down to point 6, it states: "I am not able, (a), to defend these people." And just your assessment, is that correct or incorrect? Was DutchBat in a position to defend all these people crowded in the area of the base?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then point (b): "I am not able to defend my own battalion." Is that correct or incorrect, in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's corresponding with the preceding statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now, if we look up the page, under the first full paragraph there is subparagraph (b): "Next meeting on 12 July at 10.00, with representation of the refugees and the former civil and military authorities." Can you tell me now what, if anything, you did to prepare for that next meeting at 10.00 a.m., which we also saw referenced on the video of the last meeting on 11 July at night?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the recording on 12 July at 10.00 or do you mean the meeting in the evening? I've lost track.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- my fault. Let me ask that again. What did you do, if anything, to prepare for the meeting which was scheduled for the morning at 10.00 on 12 July?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to establish contact with Tuzla and with UNHCR to state our position. Besides that, I think we met briefly together with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and Major Franken to discuss matters and consider the opportunities. And at this point, I don't remember exactly what else I did. I probably took a nap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you return to the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac on 12th July?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On 12 July, I was present at the third meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who, as you remember, came from DutchBat? Which DutchBat personnel went to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and myself were present from DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember who came as representatives of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately there were three representatives. Again, Nesib Mandzic, who has been mentioned before; a female representative, I believe her name was Camila; and another representative of the male population. I think his name was Husanovic [phoen] or something like that. At any rate, there were three representatives, but none were military of the ABiH or from the official civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you know, can you tell us why there weren't representatives from the ABiH or the official civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was that they were busy planning their flight or had already fled. And representatives of the military leadership or the civilian population were not -- in our view, they were not among the refugees in Potocari, as far as we could ascertain via interpreters and ourselves when we tried to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as best as you can recall, as you sit here today, who was present at the meeting on 12th of July, representing -- or on the side of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic, General Mladic was present; Colonel Jankovic; Major Nikolic, Momir Nikolic; the interpreter Petar; and the person who was responsible for removal at the transport, I don't remember exactly, I think his name was Kosovic; somebody from the civilian authorities who was responsible for screening the refugees. That's a preliminary list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of these civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said "responsible for screening the refugees." What does that mean? What is screening the refugees?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concerned individual was introduced by General Mladic as being responsible for inspecting all male refugees for possible war crimes or criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how was this to be done? "Inspecting" is the word in the transcript, "all the male refugees for possible war crimes or criminal behaviour," this screening?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not clear during the third conversation, or during the two previous conversations either. It came up in the third conversation that this would be happening, but how and what age group and where the inspections would take place, I don't remember that -- I don't remember any elaboration on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to watch the video now, if we may, from this meeting, what we have, and that is 65 ter number 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, please. If we could start it over go again and stop it almost immediately, the people in front of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the video starts at 1 minute -- 1 hour 42 minutes, 45.6 seconds, and is stopped for a question at 1:42:50.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, in the image we see, the counter stated by His Honour, there were four men standing facing either sideways or towards the camera. From left to right again, as we look at the screen, can you tell me who you recognise on this picture?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Having lived here --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this time, at the extreme left is General Mladic, next to him is Colonel Jankovic, and then the body-guard -- excuse me, Momir Nikolic appears.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Start that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I think it will be better. Colonel, could you be kind enough to start all over again from the left. The person at the extreme left is who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Momir Nikolic. Next to him is Colonel Jankovic. And as third in front of the door, General Mladic's body-guard. And the man at the far right, I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we also have the same problem, no sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know whether there should be any sound because there seems to be nothing happening there. Let's play it back just a few screens and then forward again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can confirm that there should be sound, Your Honour. As I recall, it's the whole -- the whole clip has sound but maybe we should start at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back a few shots, a few seconds. Yes, we can start from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the video is stopped again for a question I take it at 01:43:13.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In you could tell us what you recognise in this still, Witness, who these people are?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The woman in the foreground is the woman representative, Camila, behind the man in the blue shirt; his name was something like Husanovic. And to the right next to the car is Nesib Mandzic. And there is a soldier on the left. I believe he's a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the video is stopped once more at 01:44:55.6 for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just the men we can see, the four men in this photo, I think I can safely say in the foreground is General Mladic, you've identified. Who is the man to his left, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just while we are here the other two?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the interpreter Petar and it is Commander Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the video stopped again at 01:45:07.8 for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the very end of the table on the far right there is a man with his hand up by his chin with a moustache. Do you know -- can you identify that person?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, the man responsible for the transport, transfer, Mr. Kosovic or Kozovic [phoen], something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the video has stopped again at 01:50:07.4 for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, look at this still in front of you. Let me know if you can recognise or tell us anything about the two men to the left of General Mladic, the first one is wearing a camouflage shirt, smoking a cigarette, and the person next to him is wearing a civilian shirt. Perhaps it's not a camouflage shirt. The one with the beard smoking a cigarette and then the one to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the right of General Mladic. Actually, to the left of the photo or of the still but to the right of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The man with the light-green shirt without a cigarette is the man who was responsible for the screening. The person with the cigarette sitting to his side is I believe somebody from Bratunac itself, either from the local administration or linked to the Bratunac police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I take it from your answer you don't recall or maybe you never knew, but you don't know their names?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to their names, maybe they have been presented to me but I didn't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, the video is stopped at 01:50:25.9 for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As we are looking at the video still, the man sitting across the table from you on the far right, not the civilian you've just talked about, the man in the camouflage shirt with his hands crossed, can you tell us what you remember about him, who he is?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can remember neither his name nor his function, his position, at this present moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. The man sitting to his right looking left as we look at the photo, the man wearing a suit jacket, do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person possibly also was part of the civil administration of Bratunac or was with the police, but I can say nothing more specific about this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And then finally the men, the last two men we see on the left, one taking a drink, one who is looking down the table?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know neither their names nor their positions. I do not have this in my mind at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The video stops at 1 hour 52 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. The video clip we have seen is approximately ten minutes. How long did this third meeting last in total?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it lasted half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We were able to watch it but how did you feel during this meeting? You've told us about the previous two. What were your feelings in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the idea attempts were being made for finding a solution to provide for the evacuation of the refugees. This was a positive aspect in my feelings. However, there was unclarity as to the meaning of the word "screening," something that we didn't see in the footage, was something that concerned me. As you have seen, once or twice, people stood up for reasons of internal communications about a certain situation. This made the meeting quite nervous one. In addition, very regularly caterpillar vehicles would drive by the compound or the hotel. In the distance there also was the sound of firing. So, in general, I wouldn't describe the situation as quiet or stable. Also the outcome of the meeting was not completely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of follow-up questions. You said people stood up for reasons of internal communications about a certain situation. Can you describe that more? What was the situation you're referring to? And who stood up?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: One or two soldiers entered the meeting room from outside. They made a rather tense impression and wanted to say something. Incidents were taking place that needed immediate response, and for this reason, General Krstic, for instance, was called out of the meeting. He in his turn called other people out of the meeting. This was something I could clearly observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you explain what you mean when you said the outcome of the meeting was not completely clear. Expand -- expound on that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one question, for instance, which was transport. This matter still had to be dealt with. It wasn't clear whether the UN command or somebody else would have to do this. The fuel matter was urgent as well. Also the question of how the care for the civilian population would have to be provided. So at least for me, these issues were not resolved by clear agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did you do after the meeting ended? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned to Potocari, together with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, and there we shortly discussed the results of the meeting. We looked at the agreements. Also Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and I had to check the agreements because we hadn't been in the same position vis-a-vis the interpreter, and therefore we wanted to make sure we had a clear picture of what had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you have a clear picture after you had compared notes, as I'll put it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As to agreements, what had been agreed upon, what not, what had been promised by General Mladic and what had not, was not completely clear to myself, neither to Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, and he then asked me to immediately drive back to Bratunac to check up, check on the number of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then drove back to Bratunac, to the Hotel Fontana and I attempted to establish contact. After trying to find out some things, I ran into Major Nikolic, who said that everything had been agreed upon, that I should get lost, that there was no business of mine here, that things had already started, and that I should leave immediately. He very clearly was not at all appreciating my return. I then drove back, and already saw that coaches were driving from Bratunac into the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was there any other VRS officer, if you recall, with Momir Nikolic when you saw him and he told you what you've just explained, to get lost?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that also the gentleman with the moustache responsible for transport was present there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that the one you've referred to as Kosovic or Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Two minutes to the end, Your Honour. It would be a good time for me. I'm sorry I didn't finish today. I'll finish before the next break tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Colonel, just to put you in the picture, you heard me before asking the Defence teams to indicate approximately how much time they require to go through the various seven cross-examinations. And I have roughly an indication that it would take about eight hours. So you can count on another three days of testimony. In other words, that's tomorrow, and then Monday and on Tuesday, and hopefully we should finish with you on Tuesday. Thank you for understanding. And we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25 Blank pages 1978 to 2005 inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts (the English subtitles from the video were not transcribed in the present document)
